section_summary: This section covers internal U.S. State Department records, intelligence assessments, diplomatic reports, and translations spanning late 1941 through August 1942 concerning Japanese politics and foreign policy. Major subjects include Japanese imperial expansionist ideology and the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, the formation and outlook of the Tojo Cabinet, and U.S. governmental debates over public speeches by recently retired diplomats. It also incorporates analyses of Japan's ruling political and military cliques, wartime radio addresses celebrating Southeast Asian conquests, and Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's comprehensive post-repatriation report on Japanese wartime domestic and external developments.

subfiles.about: Concluding pages of an analytical study examining Japanese national psychology, emotional extremes, suicidal impulses, and official bureaucracy.
subfiles.summary: Report concludes on Japanese psychology: high suicide rates among patriots and officials, contrasting severe self-discipline with emotional outbursts, and pervasive rigid bureaucratism governing civic life.
subfiles.title: Study of Japanese Psychology and Bureaucracy (Conclusion)

subfiles.about: State Department Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing an intelligence report on Japanese continental policy.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (E.D. Poole)
subfiles.summary: FE summarizes an ONI article on Japan's continental policy tracing back to Komura's 1901 proposals, emphasizing fused continental-naval strategy against the U.S. and Britain.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Continental Policy Article

subfiles.about: Office of Naval Intelligence memorandum transmitting an English translation of Takehiko Okuhira's article on Japanese continental policy.
subfiles.from: Head of Foreign Intelligence Branch, Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department
subfiles.summary: The Office of Naval Intelligence forwards a translation of an article by Takehiko Okuhira published in the magazine Tairiku. Okuhira provides a comprehensive survey of Japan's continental and southward advance policies from the Meiji era to the Tripartite Pact with Germany and Italy. He examines Japan's relations with Nanking, the Thailand-Indochina border arbitration, naval supremacy in the Western Pacific, and the ideological crusade to expel Anglo-American influence from Asia.
subfiles.title: Japanese Continental Policy (Article Translation)
subfiles.to: Orme Wilson, Liaison Officer, Department of State

subfiles.about: Confidential intelligence report outlining General Wu Yi-ping's observations in Tokyo regarding the newly formed Tojo Government.
subfiles.summary: Report on Wu Yi-ping's Tokyo mission for Wang's regime notes Konoye's/Navy's moderating influence, the Emperor's Navy-consultation injunction, desire to prolong Washington talks, and Tojo's coolness toward Nanking.
subfiles.title: The New Japanese Government's Policy: Nanking Information

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum discussing former Consul General O. Gaylord Marsh's public speeches on Japan and the risks to Americans awaiting repatriation.
subfiles.summary: FE warns ex-Consul Marsh's inflammatory lectures risk Japanese retaliation against Americans awaiting repatriation, recommending he refrain from speaking until colleagues are evacuated.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Public Address by Mr. O. Gaylord Marsh

subfiles.about: Department of State draft letter requesting that retired Consul General O. Gaylord Marsh refrain from public lectures offensive to Japan.
subfiles.from: E. Wilder Spaulding, Chairman, Publications Committee
subfiles.summary: Draft letter asks Marsh to avoid offensive language in public addresses until American civilians are repatriated from Japanese territory.
subfiles.title: Draft Letter to O. Gaylord Marsh concerning Public Addresses

subfiles.about: Memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck dissenting from the total prohibition of public speeches by O. Gaylord Marsh.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck declines to muzzle Marsh, arguing no evacuation timetable exists and democracy needs an informed public, recommending marked manuscript deletions instead.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Proposed Letter to Mr. Marsh

subfiles.about: Letter from retired Consul General O. Gaylord Marsh submitting his lecture script on Japan for State Department review.
subfiles.summary: Marsh submits his blunt speech on Japan conditions, explaining it aims to awaken Americans to wartime threats, requesting approval with reservations.
subfiles.title: Letter from O. Gaylord Marsh to the Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Letter from the Department of State to O. Gaylord Marsh returning his lecture text with objectionable passages marked for omission.
subfiles.from: E. Wilder Spaulding, Chairman, Publications Committee
subfiles.summary: Committee tells Marsh his war-effort speeches are welcome but must remove offensive terms marked in red, until civilians are evacuated from Japanese areas.
subfiles.title: Letter to O. Gaylord Marsh concerning Public Addresses on Japan

subfiles.about: American Consulate General Shanghai despatch enclosing a memorandum of conversation with Asano Bussan Company Director Yasuto Shudo.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: Lockhart transmits Groves's Shanghai conversation with Shudo describing economic shortages and unrest under Konoye, and secret Konoye efforts to arrange a Roosevelt meeting via an emissary and Asano.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 829: Memorandum of Conversation with Yasuto Shudo

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs transmittal note forwarding the FCC transcript of Premier Hideki Tojo's address to the House of Peers.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Laurence E. Salisbury)
subfiles.summary: Salisbury forwards Tojo's March 1942 Peers address, flagging passages on Axis collaboration and policy toward India and Australia.
subfiles.title: Transmittal of Premier Hideki Tojo's Address of March 12, 1942

subfiles.about: Radio broadcast transcript of Premier Hideki Tojo's address to the House of Peers reviewing Axis military victories and warning India and Australia.
subfiles.summary: Premier Hideki Tojo reports to the House of Peers on the fall of the Netherlands East Indies and the capture of Rangoon, marking the severance of the Burma Road. He warns Australia that continued resistance will lead to catastrophe and urges the people of India to seize the moment to free themselves from British rule and join the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. Tojo praises Axis cooperation with Germany and Italy while warning the Japanese public against overconfidence.
subfiles.title: Speech of Premier General Hideki Tojo Delivered at House of Peers
subfiles.to: House of Peers and the Japanese public

subfiles.about: Government intelligence monograph analyzing the four dominant ruling cliques controlling Japanese political and economic life.
subfiles.summary: This intelligence report examines the four traditional power cliques (batsu) in Japanese society: the zaibatsu (financial monopolies such as Mitsui, Mitsubishi, and Sumitomo), gumbatsu (military leaders), mombatsu (hereditary court nobility), and kambatsu (higher bureaucrats). It traces their historical origins, mechanisms of political and economic dominance, and inter-factional rivalries. The report identifies popular resentment against these oligarchies as potential vulnerabilities for Allied psychological warfare.
subfiles.title: Japan's Cliques: The "Batsu"

subfiles.about: FBI confidential memorandum forwarding the views of the Spanish Minister in Shanghai regarding the Tojo Cabinet and Japanese military plans.
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.summary: Hoover relays Spanish Minister Maldonado's report calling Tojo's rise a military triumph, the army pro-German and navy reluctant, noting economic distress and a million troops poised against Siberia/Sakhalin.
subfiles.title: Opinion of Spanish Minister in Shanghai regarding Japanese Affairs
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's general report on Japanese developments after Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Max W. Bishop)
subfiles.summary: Bishop summarizes Grew's post-repatriation report: Japan attacked without Axis consultation, cautious Soviet policy to avoid a northern front, and domestic hardship with determined civilian morale.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Ambassador Grew's Post-Outbreak Report

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch and comprehensive report by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew surveying Japanese foreign relations and internal developments after December 1941.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew submits a comprehensive general report written aboard the diplomatic exchange ship MS Gripsholm following his internment and departure from Tokyo. The report opens with a detailed index and analyzes Japan's foreign relations with Axis partners, noting that Germany and Italy were not consulted prior to the December 8 attack. It further details Japanese-Soviet relations, emphasizing mutual adherence to the Neutrality Pact, the conclusion of the 1942 fisheries modus vivendi, and oil operations in northern Sakhalin.
subfiles.title: A General Report on Events and Developments in Japan after the Outbreak of War
